title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable
rights: Original instructor-authored practice; reproducible hypothetical datasets; not College Board questions

items.prompt: Nine workshop travel times, in minutes, are 5, 8, 10, 12, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18. Calculate the sample mean in minutes. Enter a number rounded to two decimal places.
items.hint: Add all nine times, then divide by nine.
items.solution: The total is 110 minutes and $n=9$. The sample mean is $\bar{x}=\frac{110}{9}\approx12.22$ minutes. It describes the average in this sample.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: Four ordered test scores are 6, 8, 11 and 12. Find the median.
items.hint: For an even sample size, average the two middle observations.
items.solution: The middle pair is 8 and 11, so the median is $\frac{8+11}{2}=9.5$ points. The median can fall between observed scores.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: Seven ordered distances, in kilometres, are 4, 5, 7, 7, 9, 11, 13. Using the median-of-halves method that EXCLUDES the overall median, calculate the interquartile range (IQR), in kilometres.
items.hint: Remove the overall median before splitting into halves; find the medians of the lower and upper triples.
items.solution: The median is 7 km. The lower half gives $Q_1=5$ km; the upper half gives $Q_3=11$ km. Thus $\mathrm{IQR}=11-5=6$ km.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: A sample of three daily temperatures, in °C, is 2, 4, 6. Find the SAMPLE VARIANCE. Enter the numerical value in °C².
items.hint: The mean is 4; squared deviations are 4, 0 and 4. Divide their sum by n − 1.
items.solution: The mean is $4\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the squared deviations total $8\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}^2$. The sample variance is $s^2=\frac{8}{3-1}=4\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}^2$. The sample standard deviation is $s=\sqrt{4}=2\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: A sample of waiting times has sample standard deviation $s=4.2$ minutes. Which interpretation is best?

options.label: A
options.text: The longest wait was exactly 4.2 minutes.

options.label: B
options.text: Waiting times typically deviate from their sample mean by about 4.2 minutes.

options.label: C
options.text: Half of the patients waited exactly 4.2 minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: The sample variance must equal 4.2 minutes.

items.hint: Standard deviation describes spread around a mean, and its units match the variable.
items.solution: B. Standard deviation describes a typical scale of deviations around the sample mean, not a maximum, median, or exact mean absolute deviation. Variance would have squared units.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: A sample mean travel time is 15 minutes. The same observations are now reported in seconds. What is the sample mean in SECONDS?
items.hint: Each observation is multiplied by 60; the mean follows the same multiplicative conversion.
items.solution: $15\text{ minutes}\times60\frac{\text{seconds}}{\text{minute}}=900\text{ seconds}$. The sample SD, median, range and IQR also multiply by 60; variance multiplies by $60^2=3600$.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: A data sample has ordered values 4, 5, 7, 7, 9, 11, 30. Which statement is correct using the median-of-halves quartiles and both outlier screens?

options.label: A
options.text: 30 is an IQR outlier but not a two-standard-deviation outlier.

options.label: B
options.text: 30 is a two-standard-deviation outlier but not an IQR outlier.

items.hint: Find Q1 = 5, Q3 = 11, and the IQR upper fence; also check mean + 2 × sample SD.
items.solution: C. The IQR is 6 and the upper fence is $11+1.5(6)=20$, so 30 is outside. The mean is $\bar{x}=\frac{73}{7}\approx10.43$ and $s\approx8.942$. Thus $\bar{x}+2s\approx28.31$, so 30 also exceeds the two-SD boundary. Both rules identify an observation to investigate.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: For the sample 4, 5, 7, 7, 9, 11, 30, calculate the UPPER two-standard-deviation screening boundary x̄ + 2s. Use SAMPLE standard deviation and round to two decimals.
items.hint: Mean is 73/7; sample standard deviation is approximately 8.94161.
items.solution: The mean is $\bar{x}=\frac{73}{7}\approx10.42857$; $s^2\approx79.95238$ and $s\approx8.94161$. The upper boundary is $\bar{x}+2s\approx10.42857+2(8.94161)\approx28.31179$, or 28.31. Because $30>28.31$, the value is flagged.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: Two independent samples of workshop travel times (minutes) are recorded. Group A has median 14 and IQR 4; Group B has median 14 and IQR 8. Compare center and spread in context, then state one conclusion that these summaries do NOT justify.
items.hint: Name the group, variable and units; compare both the medians and the IQRs numerically; do not infer population differences or causes.
items.solution: Both groups' observed median workshop travel time was 14 minutes. Group B's middle 50% of travel times was more variable (IQR 8 minutes versus Group A's 4 minutes), twice the IQR. These sample summaries do not, by themselves, prove a population difference or a causal effect, and do not completely specify the distribution's shape.
items.rubric: Full-credit self-check: (1) states equal medians of 14 minutes for the two groups; (2) states Group B has larger spread using both IQR values and units; (3) identifies a justified limitation, such as no causal claim, no population inference without design/uncertainty, or no complete distribution shape from these summaries alone.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School independently authored hypothetical exercise, 2026-10-14

items.prompt: A student is at approximately the 90th percentile for completion time in a sample, and a different sample of incomes is strongly right-skewed with some extreme values. Which statement is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: About 90% of completion times are at or below the student's time; median and IQR often summarize the skewed incomes more robustly.

options.label: B
options.text: The student completed 90% of the task; the mean and standard deviation can never change with outliers.

options.label: C
options.text: Exactly 90% of the sample must have a smaller time with no ties; the range resists extreme incomes.

options.label: D
options.text: A 90th percentile is always the largest observation; the mean is the best summary for every income distribution.

items.hint: Percentiles describe relative position, not percentage completed. Which summaries are resistant to extreme observations?
items.solution: A. A 90th percentile is a position with approximately 90% of observations at or below that value, depending on ties and the percentile convention. The median and IQR are generally resistant to extreme incomes, unlike the mean, range, and SD.
